items.title: The 30-second waits in the web test
items.body:
The goal is to find the deliberately long waits in the browser test and say what they protect against. The keyed Check points at `{ timeout: 30000 }` on lines 64 and 67 of `apps/web/test/backlog-stale-assignment.test.jsx`, and explains them: Testing Library's one-second default flaked on a slow host, so the wait was raised while the assertions stayed the same.

The grep Check reconciles the test count (13 + 4 = 17), and the `__realClient` Check explains how the nonmember test proves no mutation. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: The token in the predicate picks exactly one winner
items.body:
Both requests carry the same `expectedUpdatedAt`. The first write to commit matches the predicate and advances `updatedAt`. The second write's `updateMany` now looks for the OLD timestamp, matches zero rows, and `changed.count === 0` throws a conflict (409). The test checks `[r1.status, r2.status].sort()` equals `[200, 409]`, that the winner's timestamp changed, and that the issue sits in one of the two sprints.

- "Two 200s" is the lost-update bug a version check exists to stop.
- "Two 409s" is wrong: serializable isolation aborts at most the conflicting one, and the predicate lets the first through.
- "Retried until it also wins" is wrong: a retry reruns with the same old token and still matches zero rows.

items.title: A foreign destination is simply not found
items.body:
In `completeSprint`, the destination is looked up with `where: { id: destination, projectId: project.id }`. A sprint of another project does not match, so `target` is null and `notFound('Destination sprint')` is thrown. That throw comes before `tx.sprint.updateMany`, the first write, so the source sprint stays ACTIVE and its issues stay assigned. The regression reads both back after the 404.

- "409 only to a planned sprint" is the answer for a destination in the SAME project that is not PLANNED.
- "200 with issues moved across projects" is the bug the pre-change code had.
- "Completes with movedCount 0" is wrong because nothing is written once the lookup fails.

items.title: Checking that every refusal precedes the first write
items.body:
The goal is about ORDER: no rejection may happen after `completeSprint` has started writing. The matching Check lists every `throw` before line 114 (lines 83, 85, 89, 95 and 97) and notes that all of them run before `tx.sprint.updateMany`, the first write. It then names the regression that proves the same thing from outside: after a 404 for a cross-project destination, the source sprint is still ACTIVE and the issue is still assigned.

The diff Check is for the exercise about the pre-change gaps, and the predicate-classification Check is for the exercise that sorts predicates into scope, lifecycle and unfinished work.

items.title: The race test judges the final state
items.body:
The goal: confirm the assignment-versus-completion answer is checked on final state, not on the response. The keyed Check points at lines 268-274 of the sprint test: the assignment may return 200 or 409, and afterwards the test reads the issue detail and requires `sprintId` to be null. A test that looked only at the assignment status would miss a stranded issue.

The `toBe(captured.getTime() + 1)` Check is for the future-clock goal, and the `attempt < 3` Check is for the retry-helper goal. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: Start here: sprint assignment and completion under concurrency
items.body:
This quest studies one service file: `apps/api/src/services/sprint.service.js` in a Jira-like app. Two writes matter most. `assignIssueToSprint` moves an issue into a sprint (or back to the backlog), and `completeSprint` closes an ACTIVE sprint and moves its unfinished issues somewhere else. Both can run at the same time for the same data, so the code layers several protections.

Read in this order. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md` follows one request from the backlog page to the database. `02-CONCEPTS.md` separates isolation, state guards and stale-edit tokens. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` walks completion line by line. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` and `07-TRACE-LAB.md` show the race tests. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` checks the answers against source.

Each chapter ends with Goal/Check exercises. Several quiz questions ask which Check belongs to which Goal, so read those lists carefully.

excerpts.quote: The service is the point where project membership, allowed action, destination state, and persistence meet.

readMore.why: The hop-by-hop table from BacklogPage.jsx to the service.
The whole sprint service: read loadProject and serializable first.

items.title: Computing the next token with a fast stored clock
items.body:
The goal: compute the next token when the stored timestamp is ahead of the clock. The keyed Check points at the test that sets `updatedAt` to `Date.now() + 60_000` and expects exactly `captured.getTime() + 1`, and explains why: `Math.max(Date.now(), previous + 1)` picks the second argument because the wall clock is a minute behind.

The line-137 Check labels the three protection mechanisms, and the `updateIssue` Check compares the two writers that use `expectedUpdatedAt`. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: A state-qualified update claims the transition
items.body:
Both requests may read the sprint as ACTIVE. The claim, though, is `tx.sprint.updateMany({ where: { id: sprint.id, projectId: project.id, state: 'ACTIVE' }, ... })`. Only one request can change the row from ACTIVE to COMPLETED. The other matches zero rows and throws `conflict('Sprint was already completed')`, so it never reaches the bulk issue move.

- "Both 200, second with movedCount 0" is wrong: the loser throws before returning anything.
- "Every issue moved twice" is wrong for the same reason.
- "Waits on a lock, then succeeds" is wrong: even after waiting, its predicate no longer matches.

excerpts.quote: if (completed.count === 0) throw conflict('Sprint was already completed');

items.title: Only P2034 is retried
items.body:
`retryable` is true only for a `PrismaClientKnownRequestError` whose `code === 'P2034'`. For P2002 it is false, so both `if (retryable ...)` lines are skipped and `throw error;` rethrows the original error on the very first attempt.

- "Retried like P2034" is wrong: the code check is an exact string comparison.
- "Converted into the domain 409" only happens after the third P2034.
- "Swallowed" is wrong: the catch block always ends in a throw or a continue.

That is why `startSprint` catches its own P2002 inside the work (lines 68-71) and maps it to a 409 there; the helper would not do it.

items.title: Exact equality pins the future-clock rule
items.body:
The goal asks you to confirm that the future-clock answer is exact, not approximate. The keyed Check points at `apps/api/test/sprint.test.js:111`, which uses `toBe(captured.getTime() + 1)`: strict equality, not a range. It adds why that matters: a version of line 152 using plain `Date.now()` would be about 60,000 ms off and fail.

The retry-loop Check verifies "three attempts, P2034 only", and the lines 268-274 Check verifies the assignment-versus-completion final state. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: Nonmembers get a concealing 404
items.body:
`assignIssueToSprint` starts with `loadProject(..., 'sprint:manage')`, which calls `authorize`, which calls `requireMembership`. When the user has no role in the project's member map, it throws `notFound('Project')`. The project is hidden rather than refused, so an outsider cannot learn that it exists. Because this happens before the transaction, nothing is written; the test confirms it by reading the row directly.

- "403 naming sprint:manage" is what a MEMBER with a weaker role gets from `authorize`.
- "401" would need an invalid login; the outsider is authenticated, just not a member.
- "409" is wrong: the version check is never reached.

items.title: Strict advancement without trusting the clock
items.body:
The new token is `new Date(Math.max(Date.now(), issue.updatedAt.getTime() + 1))`. When the stored value is a minute ahead, `previous + 1` is larger than the wall clock, so the result is exactly the stored value plus one millisecond. The test asserts `toBe(captured.getTime() + 1)`, an exact equality.

- "The current wall time" would move the version BACKWARDS, so an old token could match again; that is what `Math.max` prevents.
- "Unchanged" would break strict advancement: a second assignment with the same token would still match.
- "A 409" is wrong: the request sends the exact stored token, so the version check passes.

items.title: Three attempts, then a domain conflict
items.body:
In `serializable()` the loop is `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1)`. On a P2034, `if (retryable && attempt < 2) continue;` retries after attempts 0 and 1. On attempt 2 the next line runs: `throw conflict('Sprint changed during this request; refresh and try again')`, which the app maps to 409.

- "Two runs, then a raw error" miscounts the loop: there are three attempts, and P2034 is never rethrown raw.
- "Reruns until one commits" ignores the loop bound.
- "A generic 500" is what an unrecognized error could become; P2034 is recognized and turned into the domain conflict.

items.title: Compare-then-write versus a guarded write
items.body:
`updateIssue` reads the issue, compares `issue.updatedAt.toISOString()` with the token in JavaScript, and only later runs `tx.issue.update({ where: { id: issue.id }, ... })`. Between the compare and the write, another request can pass the same compare. Both then write, and the second silently overwrites the first. Assignment avoids this by putting the token in the `updateMany` predicate, so the database checks it at write time.

- "Only to the second" is wrong: ISO strings keep milliseconds.
- "Skips when the title is missing" is wrong: the check depends only on `patch.expectedUpdatedAt`.
- "Outside any transaction" is wrong: the update and its history entry share one `$transaction`.

items.title: Labelling isolation, guards and the version check
items.body:
The goal asks you to label which lines of `assignIssueToSprint` are isolation, which are ownership or lifecycle guards, and which are the optimistic version check. The keyed Check does the labelling: isolation is the `serializable(` call (line 137); guards are the project-scoped sprint lookup and the COMPLETED rejection (lines 143-150); the version check is the `updatedAt` term in the predicate (line 156) plus `changed.count === 0` giving 409 (lines 160-162).

The `updateIssue` Check compares writers, and the 60,000 ms Check computes the next token. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: Concept: isolation, state guards and a version token are different tools
items.body:
It is tempting to say "the transaction makes it safe". This course insists on three separate ideas.

Isolation (`Serializable`) lets PostgreSQL refuse an unsafe interleaving of two transactions. When it does, Prisma reports error P2034 and the helper reruns the WHOLE transaction against a fresh view.

A state guard asks whether a row is still in the state a transition needs, for example "this sprint is still ACTIVE". Putting the state into the `where` of an `updateMany` turns a lost race into zero changed rows, which the code reports as a conflict.

A version token (`expectedUpdatedAt`) asks whether the row is still the version the browser saw. Again the strong form puts it inside the write predicate, not in an earlier read.

Ownership checks (is this sprint in this project?) are a fourth, independent rule.

excerpts.quote: A bounded retry repeats the entire transaction against a fresh view; it does not merely repeat the last statement.
Each mechanism protects a distinct invariant and should retain its own test.

readMore.why: The full assignIssueToSprint excerpt with all mechanisms in one function.

items.title: A missing token disables the check without any error
items.body:
The backlog sends `expectedUpdatedAt: issue.updatedAt`. If the list endpoint never selected `updatedAt`, that value is `undefined`, and `JSON.stringify` leaves undefined fields out of the body. The schema marks the field `.optional()`, so validation passes. In the service the predicate uses `...(expectedUpdatedAt ? { updatedAt: ... } : {})`, so with no token the stale check is simply not added. Every request would succeed and nothing would reveal the gap.

- "400" is wrong because the field is optional.
- "409 every time" assumes the token is compared; it is never added to the predicate.
- "A controller crash" is wrong: reading a missing property gives `undefined`, not an exception.

items.title: Comparing the two writers that use expectedUpdatedAt
items.body:
The goal: compare sprint assignment with the OTHER writer that uses `expectedUpdatedAt`, and judge which is stronger. The keyed Check names that writer, `updateIssue` in `issue.service.js`. It reads the issue, compares timestamps in JavaScript, and only then runs an `update` whose `where` is just `{ id }`. Because the compare is not in the write predicate, two requests can both pass it. Assignment, which puts the token in `updateMany`, is stronger.

The line-137 Check labels the three mechanisms, and the lines 96-112 Check computes the future-clock token.

excerpts.quote: The compare is not in the write predicate, so two requests can both pass it.

items.title: Sorting completion predicates by purpose
items.body:
The goal is to classify every predicate in `completeSprint`. The keyed Check does exactly that: project scope is `projectId: project.id`; lifecycle is `assertTransition`, `target.state !== 'PLANNED'` and `state: 'ACTIVE'`; unfinished work is `columnId: { notIn: doneColumnIds }`. It also asks why the bulk move needs no project filter: `sprintId: sprint.id` names a sprint that was already found inside the project.

The diff Check answers the "what did the old version get wrong" exercise, and the throws-before-line-114 Check answers the ordering exercise. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

excerpts.quote: where: { sprintId: sprint.id, columnId: { notIn: doneColumnIds } },

items.title: Concept: the database owns the one-active-sprint rule
items.body:
Some rules can be checked by looking at one row: a sprint must be PLANNED before it starts, and it needs at least one issue. Those live in a small state machine, `apps/api/src/domain/sprint-state-machine.js`, as a table of transitions.

Other rules span rows: "at most one ACTIVE sprint per project". Two requests can each read "no other sprint is active" and both proceed, so an application check cannot enforce it. The migration therefore creates a PARTIAL unique index that applies only to ACTIVE rows. The service has to catch the database's refusal and translate it into a clean HTTP response instead of letting a raw error escape.

When you read `startSprint`, look for where that translation happens and which Prisma error code it expects.

excerpts.quote: holds. Here: at most one ACTIVE sprint per project, but any number of PLANNED
per-sprint rules; the DB owns the cross-sprint invariant.

items.title: Why the nonmember test reads the database directly
items.body:
The goal: explain why the nonmember test reads through `__realClient` and not through the API. The keyed Check gives the reason: the outsider's API reads would return 404 just like the write did, so the API cannot show what happened to the row. Querying `__realClient.issue.findUnique` directly is the only way to show that neither `sprintId` nor `updatedAt` changed.

The 30-second timeout Check belongs to the web-test exercise, and the grep Check reconciles the test count with the evidence log. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

excerpts.quote: const stored = await __realClient.issue.findUnique({ where: { id: i1.id } });

items.title: Report what the write actually did
items.body:
Chapter 03 lists four gaps in the old `completeSprint`. Gap (d): `movedCount` came from a `count()` taken BEFORE the move, so it reported what the code expected to move rather than what it did move. Today the service returns `movedCount: moved.count`, the result of the bulk `updateMany` itself, inside the same transaction.

- "From the updateMany result" describes the current code, not the old one.
- "From the number of DONE columns" confuses the filter with the result: DONE column ids only select which issues are unfinished.
- "From the sprint's _count after completion" is wrong: `_count` is used by `startSprint` for its issue guard, not by completion.

excerpts.quote: (d) `movedCount` came from a `count()` taken before the move, not from the move's own result.

items.title: The constraint, not the state machine, decides
items.body:
Each start updates a different row (s1 or s2), and each sprint passes its own state-machine guard (PLANNED, has issues). The only rule that sees both rows is the database's partial unique index `Sprint_one_active_per_project`. The second update violates it, Prisma raises P2002, and `startSprint` catches exactly that code and throws `conflict('Another sprint is already active in this project')`.

- "The state machine refuses" is wrong: it only checks per-sprint rules.
- "Both start" is what would happen without the index.
- "Retried into a 500" is wrong: a P2034 retry would hit the same constraint or exhaust into a 409, never a 500.

items.title: Match your timeline to the real assertions
items.body:
The goal: make sure your two-column timeline matches what the never-strands test actually asserts. The keyed Check lists those assertions: completion must return 200 (line 268), the assignment may return 200 or 409 (line 269), and the final `sprintId` must be null (line 274). If your timeline ends with the issue still on the completed sprint, find the guard that prevents it: the COMPLETED check in the service or the serialization conflict.

The other Check explains the different concurrent-starts test, where the unique index, not a retry, produces the 409.

items.title: Reconciling the test count with the evidence
items.body:
The goal is to reconcile the course's test count with the recorded evidence. The keyed Check counts top-level `it(` blocks: `grep -c` prints 13 for `apps/api/test/sprint.test.js` and 4 for `apps/api/test/issue.test.js`. That is 17, the same number as the `Tests 17 passed` line in the evidence log. Counting yourself is how you check a claim like "17 tests passed" instead of trusting it.

The `__realClient` Check answers the nonmember exercise, and the `{ timeout: 30000 }` Check answers the web-test exercise. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: Finding every serializable caller
items.body:
The goal is to list every service function that runs inside the serializable boundary. The keyed Check is a search: `git grep -n "return serializable("` in the sprint service prints three lines, 46, 81 and 137, one each for `startSprint`, `completeSprint` and `assignIssueToSprint`. The map chapter adds that `listSprints`, `createSprint` and `sprintReport` do not use it.

The `__NO_ROLLBACK__` Check is for the exercise about the test suite opting out of rollback isolation, and the diff Check is for the list-projection wiring gap. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

items.title: Why concurrent starts end in a 409
items.body:
The goal: explain why the concurrent-starts test expects 409 and not a serialization retry. The keyed Check gives the reason: the two starts update DIFFERENT sprint rows, so the partial unique index is what rejects the second one. That raises P2002, which `startSprint` maps to 409 at lines 68-71. Even if PostgreSQL first reports P2034, `serializable()` retries and the retry hits the same constraint or runs out of attempts; both end in 409.

The other Check, about lines 268, 269 and 274, belongs to the timeline exercise for the never-strands test.

excerpts.quote: so the partial unique index is what rejects the second one.

items.title: Completed sprints are found, then refused
items.body:
The sprint lookup is `tx.sprint.findFirst({ where: { id: sprintId, projectId: project.id } })`. It filters by project only, so a COMPLETED sprint of the same project IS found. The next line checks `sprint.state === 'COMPLETED'` and throws `conflict('Issues cannot be assigned to a completed sprint')`, a 409.

- "404 Sprint" would be the answer for a sprint of ANOTHER project; completed sprints are not hidden.
- "200" would strand work in a closed sprint, which this guard exists to prevent.
- "400 from the schema" is wrong: `assignSprintSchema` only checks that `sprintId` is a string or null.
